subject: Millennium Prize Problems
hook: MILLENNIUM PRIZE PROBLEMS IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK
angle: Although the Clay Mathematics Institute pledged $1 million for solving each of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, the only prize ever awarded was completely rejected. Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman solved the Poincaré conjecture, but turned down the $1 million bounty in 2010.
angle_support: As of 2026, the only Millennium Prize problem to have been officially declared solved is the Poincaré conjecture. The Clay Institute awarded the monetary prize to Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman in 2010. However, he declined the award

For his proof of the Poincaré conjecture, Perelman was awarded the Millennium Prize on March 18, 2010. However, he declined the award and the associated prize money, stating that Hamilton's contribution was no less than his own.
title: The Millennium Prize Problem Winner Who Refused $1 Million
description: While seven major math problems were famously selected for a million-dollar prize, the only person to ever officially win the award turned the money down. This video explores why the Poincaré conjecture's solver rejected the Clay Institute's bounty.
narration: MILLENNIUM PRIZE PROBLEMS IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK You picture a prestigious competition where brilliant minds compete to claim million-dollar rewards for solving the hardest math challenges. It was closer to a graveyard for bounties. Only one problem has ever been officially declared solved, and the winner walked away with absolutely nothing. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute designated seven monumental tasks, offering a million dollars each for a verified solution. When Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman finally conquered the Poincaré conjecture in 2003, he became the first and only person to earn the prize. However, in 2010, he formally rejected the seven-figure check. He insisted that his own contribution was equal to the foundational work of Richard Hamilton, and refused to accept an award that did not acknowledge them both as partners. The money remains unclaimed, proving some mathematicians value academic integrity far more than a massive payout.
